countries that share the problem with Canada. As the minister pointed out, it is not a uniquely Canadian problem. Price structures have been breaking down throughout the world, and Canadian farmers cannot earn a decent return on the capital that is involved. A little while ago a letter came to my hands which I find rather typical. It is from a man in Manitoba who runs a fairly good sized operation, and who wrote as follows:
At the moment our current operating debt is in the neighbourhood of $19,000 acquired over the past year and a half. Our interest charges this year have been in excess of $5,000 and farming over the past years has not been able to generate that kind of money-
He is operating 820 acres. He has about a $90,000 investment, and he is considered a model farmer in his area. He has 12,000 bushels of wheat, plus a lot of other crops, but he has no cash and he cannot meet his commitments. This is like any other industry that is going through a long-term problem to which long-term solutions must be applied. The traditional export markets have evaporated. The types of wheat in demand in the world have changed. To a large extent we are growing types of wheat that are no longer needed because milling techniques have changed. Inflation has driven up operating costs. According to an article in Maclean's magazine, which states the obvious but in a rather dramatic way, farm costs have been rising consistently. It reads:
By 1967, according to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, they were 68 per cent higher than in 1949, yet farm income was up only 9.7 per cent in the same period. On the basis of 1949 dollars, income was down by 33.1 per cent.
There is another thing which I do not think any government should try to sidestep, that is that governments in the immediate past encouraged farmers to grow everything that they could grow and told them that they could sell it. But if you look at the record, again broadly speaking, whether under the former Conservative regime or under this regime, large quantities of wheat have only been sold effectively when there has been trouble; and it is a poor type of practice in any business if you can only succeed when someone else comes a-cropper.
If you have a famine in Russia, in China or somewhere else, then the major wheat producers can unload their surpluses; otherwise they cannot. What I am trying to suggest is that we hear a lot about short-term solutions, but this government would be less than honest with people if it did not say the sort of

thing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been saying, and it would be less than conscientious if it did not go for long-term solutions.
There is no use being sentimental at the expense of the poor guy who is out on the farm and saying that we have always produced all the wheat in the world and we can always sell it in the long term, and that sooner or later it will work out; let the boys sit on their wheat for a few years and let the people of Canada carry them for a few years because one of these days the wheat will be sold. I think that is being romantic at someone else's expense. It really is time that the fundamental problem was faced.
There are several solutions to which reference is made all the time. People want two-price wheat. I do not think you can ask the people in the rest of Canada to pay extra for their bread on a long-term basis so as to keep wheat producers producing all the wheat they want, especially at a time when the trend in tariffs is down in eastern Canada and in the central markets of the world.
9 (5:10 p.m.)
We cannot have it both ways. If we encourage a tariff-protected industry in western Canada-which we have never had to this date-at the same time as we discourage tariffs in the east, we are being more schizophrenic than anybody would expect even a democratic government to be. I am all for democratic government, but we are sometimes accused of trying to buy people with their own money.
The same argument applies to acreage payments on a long-term basis. Perhaps a case can be made for acreage payments to enable people to live through an emergency, if they are tied in with a policy which encourages farmers to change from wheat to other types of production. However, I believe that long-term acreage payments for the sake of subsidizing a farmer are a dishonest approach to the solution that is required.
Rhetoric such as we have heard here all winter will not help much; neither will misquotes or partial misquotes of the Prime Minister's speeches when he goes west and makes famous statements such as, "I am not going to sell your wheat." I was there, know what he said and what he meant when he said it. If I had been a little less new at the game I would have gone right back and given the rest of his speech at every opportunity, so the message would have been conveyed loud
July 21, 1969

and clear, rather than its being sullied and misquoted for several weeks.
To illustrate that the present government is not completely ignorant of the situation and completely misunderstands it, I should like to quote from a lead editorial which appeared in the Financial Times this week, dealing with problems in the west. The editorial reads in part:
To say that there is no chance of a general and unselective payment being made to wheat farmers is to face the facts of government economics in this day and age.
This is what we have heard so much talk about: general, unselective payments with no long-term objectives in mind. I believe this type of program would do a disservice to the Canadian farmer in particular and the country as a whole. I hope the government will continue to have enough guts not to advocate such programs, but will move forward with imaginative, long-term policies that do not involve unselective payments generally.
With regard to general subsidies, the New Democratic party seem to want people to be subsidized for this, that and the other thing when the mood of the country is to try to get away from subsidies. A short time ago the Winnipeg Tribune, commented editorially on the difficulties experienced in Europe, where in the 1967-68 season because of subsidies 30,000 tons of Italian oranges were destroyed. The article continues:
This year grapes and apples have joined the waste in rivers and garbage dumps. In France and Belgium thousands of tons of potatoes, peaches, pears, cauliflowers and fish have been destroyed while the cost of living for city people has grown at an ever faster rate. The high cost of food is a major factor.
This situation developed because of the policy of subsidization that all the common market countries have been following; so let us not join our N.D.P. friends in following that Pied Piper very far. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I am not an expert on these matters, but I believe that short-term solutions to meet specific problems such as we have can be devised. In the long run these would not hurt the country as a whole. Shortterm aid is already given for drying wheat, and there are advances on unsold and undelivered grain. Further advances will be made next year, as the Prime Minister has said, amounting to millions of dollars. It is all very well to say that these advances are purely loans. They are cash infusions which, if hon. members opposite are correct, should be enough in themselves to help the situation

because their purpose is to tide people over to the time when we shall again be selling unlimited quantities of wheat to Russia.
But over and above these, there should perhaps be some form of cash subsidy for a stated length of time to help the farming industry to meet specific, long-term objectives. These objectives might be defined as diversification, rationalization of farm size and efficiency and replacement of some farm employment by industry, using government "seed" money through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, with the cooperation of provincial governments. Another solution would be the encouragement of food banks by the United Nations or other international agencies. These are long-term objectives, and any further short-term aid should be tied in with them.
I apologize again for not being an expert on these matters. We have heard a great deal in the last few months about the great government of Manitoba that was recently defeated at the polls, what a terrific job they were doing and what a lousy job everybody else was doing. We have been told how terribly difficult it was to get Ottawa to pay any attention to them. According to a brief presented to the Manitoba legislature by the Meat Packers Council of Canada last May, within the province of Manitoba itself lies the solution to at least part of its agricultural problem; yet the province did precisely nothing about it.
This is why it is very important to take a long-term view of these problems and to achieve co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in working out policies which are of lasting benefit, rather than shouting names at each other. Hog production in Manitoba has seriously declined, as has cattle production. They are not producing nearly as many cattle and hogs as they should be. The province has the capacity to improve their situation, with federal government help, presumably, if they ask for it and if they have plans that are worth considering and can be used as a basis for co-operation.
Iowa produces 22 million hogs a year. Manitoba, which has about the same population as Iowa and is about the same area, produces only 750,000. North America is a huge meat market and there is no reason for Manitoba producing so few hogs. The Manitoba meat industry is working to only about 65 per cent capacity, mainly for two reasons. The first is that Manitoba farmers are not producing enough cattle and hogs, and there

July 21, 1969
Wheat Export Prices
is not within their shipping area a market of sufficient size for the packing houses. Second, they are not producing cattle or hogs of the quality required.
Many farmers in Manitoba are primarily concerned with dairy products and sell "on the side" the cattle they do not need. There are exceptions, of course, but statistically this is true. Somebody will have to take steps to upgrade the industry in that province and obtain a sizeable proportion of the available market. Manitoba has less than one per cent of the North American hog market, and approximately one per cent of the cattle market. This is one reason for the decline in the industry. From the point of view of quality, 43 per cent of hogs produced in Canada are graded A; in Manitoba only 35 per cent are graded A. The same is true of meat: 56 per cent of cattle slaughtered in Canada are graded as red or blue beef; in Manitoba the figure is 47 per cent.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Manitoba's average is considerably below the national average, both in quality and quantity. Instead of bleating about wheat production and inability to sell, some federal action should be taken in co-operation with the provincial government to improve grades and achieve 100 per cent production capacity. If necessary, more plants should be built to reach a future 100 per cent capacity. The market potential is well-nigh unlimited, but quality must be improved and the product merchandised, the same as with other commodities. But as I say, there must be co-operation between the federal and provincial governments toward these ends.
If this immediate past history of the late provincial government of Manitoba means anything at all, it is indicative of a lot of time-wasting and wringing of hands instead of tackling problems that exist. I guess the late government has now received its just deserts.
I do not have any easy solutions. As I say, even the four major wheat producing countries of the world cannot seem to find solutions. However, I do think that short-term cash infusions are required, and I hope such infusions will be increased. We also need long-term, well thought out plans. Even if we have to listen to the opposition criticise our "inaction" for another six months we would do better to stick to sound principles and prepare some long-term plans to assist the west to return to what it should be, a farming 
community though not necessarily a predominantly wheat farming one. If we have to take another few million acres out of wheat production, this is not going to be a long-term tragedy. Let us not be romantic about the fact that because we have always grown millions of bushels of wheat we will have to continue to do so, even though the poor farmer has absolutely no way of making an economic living therefrom.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is but one of a number held this session on agriculture, particularly on agricultural problems in western Canada. Many of the arguments and statements that have been put forward today are a repetition of the arguments addressed since last September. A number of times Your Honour has been requested to grant an emergency debate, and in your wisdom on most occasions Your Honour has ruled it out because the matter had already been brought up repeatedly. I trust Your Honour will understand that we of the opposition have felt obligated, as one of our responsibilities, to keep raising the question, no matter how inconvenient it may be or how untimely or uncomfortable for people in some places. This is an issue that affects the entire nation. It is not narrowly confined to just one or two provinces; all of Canada is affected.
I was hoping that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) would have some announcement to make about new government initiatives to deal with Canada's agricultural problems, particularly in the area of immediate concern today, western Canadian cereal grains and world markets. The minister spoke of it being an international problem, and of course it is. He has told us nothing that we did not already know.
I submit that the minister is incapable of dealing with the problem or of taking new initiatives to find solutions. I say this because when the minister goes to Washington or to Winnipeg he is handcuffed by the government of Canada's lack of policy. In this way the Canadian Wheat Board as well as the minister have been continually handcuffed for the past year. Until the government of this country takes new initiatives and introduces new policies to enable the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Canadian Wheat Board to do the kind of job of which they are capable, there will be no quick solution or improvement to the present situation.
It is all very well for the minister and for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to talk
July 21, 1969

about an objective of 1,300 million bushels of wheat sales in three years, or whatever the figure is. It is, of course, good to have objectives, but unless the government has the policies to achieve such objectives, or to give some reasonable chance of achieving them, they are all to no avail.
The Prime Minister's recent trip to western Canada, uncomfortable although it may have been for him, is the most recent example of the kind of callous disregard there is for the wheat farmers, as well as an illustration of the government's complete failure to understand the size of the problem, let alone its immediacy. The remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) illustrated this in a first class manner. The hon. member does not comprehend the size of the problem, let alone its immediacy. Only when the government declares that agriculture is a primary industry that is basic to the health and wealth of the entire Canadian economy, and takes action accordingly, will some shortterm and long-term policies be forthcoming.
Mr. Speaker, a question of privilege.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, it did not seem to me that I had indicated that I had no realization that agriculture was a major industry. What I was trying to express, though it may have been difficult for some members to comprehend my remarks, perhaps because I spoke badly or perhaps because of a natural disadvantage, was that agriculture was a major industry, one that had to be given serious consideration. I said that perhaps the emphasis within the industry should be redirected. I was not advocating that agriculture be neglected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is hardly raising a question of privilege. I think the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) should be allowed to continue his remarks.

This is a fresh illustration that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, like a lot of his colleagues, does not understand the totality of the problem. The hon. member talked about diversification and referred to hogs and cattle. The farmers have been hearing this kind of talk from Liberals for the last 25 years. One has only to go back to the 1950's when the plea was for diversification. The farmers diversified their
Wheat Export Prices
operations, and what happened to hog and cattle prices? We were up to our eyes in hogs. We were told that too many hogs were being raised.
The hon. gentleman expects the farmers to diversify their operations and compete with corporate enterprises. I would ask the hon. member if he is prepared to support measures to prohibit corporate enterprise operating farms? If he is, then I will believe that he does understand the problems of the farming industry. We are not talking about a private corporation and its board of directors. We are talking about farmers who work on the land, about people, not corporations. This is what the government, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre still do not understand.
During his trip out west last week the Prime Minister made reference to income protection and mentioned a number of measures that, are supposed to ensure income protection. First of all, the Prime Minister felt somewhat insulted by some of the signs and yelling at some of the meetings held in Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister may find things difficult when he arrives at a place where nobody loves him, but I suggest he will become increasingly aware of this sort of thing unless he quits shrugging his shoulders and starts rubbing his shoulders with the problems confronting Canada.
I may say that the kind of demonstration carried on last week by the farmers of western Canada is unusual and extremely rare. Demonstrating is not something that they are prone to do, unlike some people in large urban centres. The farmers are just not built that way. They never have been. If ever there was a sign of outrage, of their extreme disgust and despair, then this was it. The prairie farmers do not make a habit of that kind of demonstration. But for years they have been back and forth to Ottawa with resolutions, briefs and agricultural delegations. At times, when they have become desperate, they have elected a few Liberals, but to no effect. All the time they have received the run around. The government which has refused to face facts, has victimized them. This government has not taken into account the fact that the Canadian agricultural community is basic to the nation's welfare and that western problems cannot be treated as separate problems. The Prime Minister has talked about income protection, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Credit Corporation. Well, farmers do not need more loans. They have debts

July 21, 1969
Wheat Export Prices
enough already. And what did the amendments to farm legislation that the Prime Minister spoke about accomplish? In the end, the result of those measures was to raise the interest rates that farmers have to pay from 5 to 7J per cent.
e (5:30 p.m.)
Mention has been made of cash advances. It seems that all those on the government side have forgotten these must be paid back. The more you advance to a farmer, the more he must pay back. Opposition parties share the government's view that cash advances are necessary. The opposition spent years trying to persuade Liberals to implement those advances, and only after they were defeated in the late 1950's did they become converts to the idea. Although these advances are interest free, they must nevertheless be paid back. The farmer, in fact has not had income protection but he, in common with his fellow Canadians, has been victimized by parasitic, high interest rates. The farmer has been victimized also by the private grain trade, and I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) will agree with me, I submit that this private trade in grain should be subject to controls. These traders have been parasites on the backs of the Canadian agricultural community for too many years.
The Prime Minister talks about income protection at a time when grain prices are low and about to go lower. Bearing these factors in mind, our party proposed a cash deficiency payment program of, say, 20 cents per bushel to be based on deliveries in the 1967-68 crop year, for a maximum of $2,000 in each case. What was the government's response to that? Nothing. It has made no response. If our suggestion is no good let the government explain why it thinks so. Over two dozen proposals have been made by opposition spokesmen, and we are still waiting for the government's reaction to them.
The Prime Minister asks how he can give "X" million dollars to the farmers when he must also consider fishermen and pensioners. He asks, how will he explain it to these other elements, in the population. We are not asking him to explain anything to the farmers, fishermen, pensioners or the unemployed. We want him to explain why he can do nothing for farmers, fishermen, pensioners or the unemployed at a time when his Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will be sitting on his fat surplus of $250 million for this fiscal year. The Prime Minister says nothing about bank

profits or outrageously increased corporate profits. Why do the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and all the other mouthpieces on the government side, talk about fighting inflation and then hurt the people who are not causing inflation. Farmers who have no cash cannot contribute to inflation. Fishermen, pensioners and the unemployed are not guilty of contributing to inflation, on the other hand, all the so-called bastions of private enterprise that contribute to inflation are aided and abetted by this incompetent government.
May I make a few suggestions to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? To implement them he will need the authority of the government, because neither he nor the Wheat Board can do very much unless the government changes its policies substantially. I hope the minister will go to the cabinet and say, "Let's give these suggestions a try." I hope he goes to caucus and says, "These are the measures you must adopt; if you do not go along with me, get yourself a new boy." If he does that, he will go down in our history as the minister who struck a blow for our farmers.
I suggest that the minister ought to go to the Prime Minister and his colleagues in cabinet and say that the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board must be tremendously extended, and that we must provide it with finances that will enable it to undertake the export of our wheat in competition with other countries. If necessary, let us wage an export war. Countries that break their agreements have victimized us. Canada did not break those agreements. If Australia wants to play games, we too can play. We can teach them a lesson or two. I say to the minister that it is unfair and immoral to leave Canadian farmers alone to compete with the treasuries of the United States and other countries. If the agricultural community of this country is left in that plight, it will be destroyed. That is quite right, and that is why I say that the Canadian Wheat Board needs financial resources to do the kind of job that must be done. If in order to sell wheat we have to cut our price to $1 a bushel, let us do so-but not at the expense of the farmer. Let us not call on our farmers to pay the whole shot. Is it not socially desirable that we maintain in Canada maximum number of economic farm units? I am sick and tired of hearing vague hints from the government side that we should have fewer farmers. Where are the farmers we take off the farm to go, Mr. Speaker?
July 21. 1969

Instead of supporting ex-farmers in metropolitan centres, is it not cheaper to help them maintain themselves on their farms?
Another suggestion is this. Could the government not enter into barter arrangements? Has the government considered seriously accepting as part payment for grain sold abroad, the currency of the country to which the grain has been sold? We could leave the currency in that country and invest it in whatever way would be best. For instance, has the minister considered the quantity of fertilizer that India needs? Would it not be a good idea to accept rupees-or the appropriate currency-in part payment for grains and use that money to build a fertilizer plant, a hospital, or whatever else is needed? Have Wheat Board officials considered these barter arrangements? Have these suggestions with respect to foreign currency been brought to their attention? Has the minister thought of authorizing the Wheat Board to wage a wheat war to meet foreign competition? If that is what our foreign competitors want, they will get it. But, surely, Mr. Speaker, this government does not expect our farmers to carry the burden of that war. Our farmers need to be backed up by the resources of the whole nation. The set back they received when the bottom dropped out of the I.G.A. was bad enough.
But it seems that the government and this country's transport industry are incapable of organizing the movement of grain to ensure even a five-bushel quota by the end of July. I may add that this five-bushel quota is the lowest in our history. May I draw to the attention of the house an instance when the minister, unknowingly misled the house? On July 3, in reply to a question raised in this house, the minister read a telegram from the Chief Commissioner of the Wheat Board, as reported at page 10784 of Hansard. I do not think I will be taking this statement out of context if I quote from the middle of the paragraph. It had to do with the grain movement. The telegram read in part:

Would further advise that both railways currently have a very substantial number of cars under load to lakehead and Pacific coast-
This is true.
-and are spotting cars for additional loads each week to the full unload capacity of the terminals.
On July 1, Mr. Speaker, the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool issued one of the strongest statements I have ever seen

from a president of that organization. He reported 10 million bushels in their terminals at the lakehead. He reported that, in order to handle their expected export or unload shipments into ships, plus filling that space, their grain company would require 11,000 box cars of grain. They would require a minimum of 440 cars a day to unload. But at that time they were unloading exactly half that number, yet the Commissioner of the Wheat Board states in his telegram that the terminals were being supplied with cars to their maximum unload capacity. That was not true then, Mr. Speaker, and is not true now.
The minister knows what kind of railway equipment is required to have a grain movement that will complete the delivery of the five-bushel quota. We all know the number of cars required. What we want to know is, are they being supplied? A few days ago, in a telephone conversation with people in the grain trade and the transportation business, we were talking about the unload capacity of the terminals. At the lakehead, on July 9, there were 3,600 carloads of grain, give or take 50 or 100. I cannot vouch for the exact figure, but that is very close. There were 3,600 carloads of grain waiting to be unloaded. Of that number, only 414 were for the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool terminals. The Saskatchewan Pool terminals, going full blast six days a week, three shifts a day, can unload over 600 cars a day. In order to fill up the space they have to handle their outgoing shipments, as well as to properly utilize a maximum staff, on overtime, going six days a week, they would require 1,200 cars.
The same situation occurred at Vancouver. One day this month they ran out of cars to unload. They worked half a day and sent the workers home. This kind of record for the grain movement indicates incompetence on the part of the government and the railroads, Mr. Speaker; there is no other way to describe it.
While half the shipping points in the three prairie provinces are all on three or four-bushel quotas, the minister is still too willing and ready to accept the assurances of the railroads that they are co-operating. Of course, they have a lot of cars for the grain movement. What else is new? I have some questions which I wish to address to the minister. I hope the minister will read a statement on motions tomorrow or Wednesday at the latest. As of now, what number of railway cars are in the grain movement? What number are required to complete the delivery of the five-bushel quota? I am sure that, as

of now, this figure is somewhere between 20,000 and 25,000 cars. The minister can get the exact figure.
What number of cars, additional to those now in the grain movement, are required from the railways between now and July 31 to complete delivery of the five-bushel quota? This could do wonders for the cash income position of the farmers. What additional number have already been supplied, compared to the number in the grain movement on July 1 ?

What action have the government and the Canadian Wheat Board taken to ensure that the terminal facilities of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool at both the lakehead and Vancouver are, in fact, being utilized to full unload capacity? Will the minister advise whether the grain companies have been authorized to buy grain after July 31? If not, will they be?
Will the minister advise if the crop year will be extended? Will the government authorize the Canadian Wheat Board to complete the purchase of a five bushel quota from farmers? They can deliver it any time in August, September, or whenever required. Will the minister discuss with the Canadian Wheat Board and the Board of Grain Commissioners the possibility of allowing offsite and offtrack storage, including the piling of wheat on the ground? Will the minister assure the Canadian Wheat Board that if there are any losses incurred as a result of this kind of handling, the tab will be picked up by the government of Canada? In that way, the minister will get the five-bushel quota delivered.
Will the minister discuss with the railways the possibility of using different kinds of railway equipment? I made a trip to the United States, through North Dakota, Minnesota and Wisconsin, a few weeks ago. I stopped in a number of rural communities to inspect their country elevators. They are not only using box cars, they are using gondola cars. At one point they had even boarded up stock cars, filling them with grain or corn. At present 
there are several hundred gondola cars, which hold almost 2,000 bushels of grain each, and which are normally used for hauling of potash, sitting idle in gravel pits and side tracks. Will the minister ask the railways to use their imagination in order to turn this and other kinds of equipment into grain moving equipment?
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) mentioned the situation in Peace River. You can go anywhere in the prairie provinces and see the same thing. We have found a consistent pattern of lack of co-operation by the railways, lack of imagination by the government, refusal by the government to authorize the Wheat Board to take extraordinary measures, because they know how to do the job. What they need from the government is authority and money.
I wish to repeat to the minister one of my earlier sentences. Surely, the minister will agree it is socially desirable to have the maximum number of people possible on the land on economic units. We do not want to hear this nonsense about less farmers. We need a government which will put the resources of the entire nation behind an industry that is basic to our whole economy. The ramifications of dropping farm income will hit the constituency of every single member in this house. Any member who does not believe that is under a great disillusion.
The ramifications of the drop in farm income over the past year and succeeding year are being felt by the farm implement industry, automobile industry, steel industry, transportation industry, fertilizer industry, building industry and lumber industry. Even the fishing industry will suffer. This is not proper. This is not civilized. It is not even good business. That phrase should appeal to hon. members across the way.
A basic industry should not be in this kind of financial condition. All we are asking the government to do is to come up with proposals, both short and long-term. We may criticize some, but we will undoubtedly support some. We may make alternative suggestions. We in this party, as well as farm organizations, have pleaded with the minister. The minister has yet to mention the latest submission from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Surely, they must have some knowledge of the subject. Proposals have been made to the minister week after week and month after month by farmers' unions, but we have yet to have any definite response
July 21. 1969



from the government as to whether they will accept any of these proposals.
If the government is not going to accept the proposals what are they going to do on their own initiative? After the experience of the Prime Minister last week, I hope the government will now wake up and bring about some positive action, if not on what the opposition parties have mentioned then on the proposals of the people engaged in the farm industry, or their own, if they have any. We have waited, and we do not want to wait much longer.

I should
like to say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I notice the absence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) from this most important debate. The honourable member had better not talk so much or they will make him a minister and keep him quieter.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) dealt particularly with subsidies as a western member. What he said was new to me and I come from a little farther west than he does. I compliment the Prime Minister on his visit
Wheat Export Prices
because he conceded there was a problem in western Canada relating directly to the wheat situation. This is what we are talking about.
It took him a long time to find out.

Yes, as my hon. friend says, it took him a long time to find out. It certainly did, but at least he came to that opinion. He found out there was a problem. During his visit he said there would be no handouts. I take it that that means subsidies. That is what my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre said.

Quoting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) page 3474 of Hansard, the 1968-69 subsidies amount to $415 million. Running down the page one can see that the quality premium on high grade hogs and lamb carcasses amounted to $110 million. Freight assistance on western feed grain totalled $21 million. So I would ask the hon member, through you, Mr. Speaker, what is all the talk about helping the western grain farmers by way of subsidies. I have not even mentioned the $80 million given away to the automobile industry. I do not know whether it is permissible to mention that in this debate, but it might be. I complimented the Prime Minister for having found a problem in the west. Some people on his side of the house do not agree.

He says the problem arises because there is overproduction of wheat and the farmers should not grow so much. I have been here for some time and was here when the Liberal party was in opposition. At that time they were saying the same thing. They ridiculed a minister of that government who said, "Grow more; we will sell it". Today, they are saying, "Do not grow it; we cannot sell it". The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Just before I called it six o'clock I referred to the absence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). I see he is present now, so perhaps I should repeat what I said. Earlier I complimented the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on his visit to the west, as a result of which he found there was a problem there. I hope you will forgive me for the time I am taking at this moment in reference to the Minister of Agriculture Mr. Speaker, who is my neighbour. Perhaps I could call him my friend. He may want to hear what I had to say earlier, in order that he might reply.
I recall the time when the minister had a great deal to say about the government, and I recall the time when he joined that government. In looking through some scrapbooks today I was reminded a little bit of the Minister of Agriculture. I have in mind particularly Throop's scrapbook at page 112. Mr. R. B. Hanson having interrupted Mr. C. G. Power, Mr. Power is reported as having said:
The hon. member had better not talk so much or they will make him a minister and keep him quieter.
I think that is what has happened to our Minister of Agriculture.
I note that the Prime Minister is not in is seat at this particular moment. How in the name of heaven can we resolve an important debate like this when the house is adjourned

for a specific purpose and the ministers responsible are not here? This whole matter also involves the rule question, but perhaps we should go into that on another day.
When the Prime Minister was out west he expressed the conclusion that there would be no handouts to people with assets of $100,000. I think the press was very kind to the Prime Minister. At one time he said they were not, but I think on his recent visit both writers and broadcasters were reasonable. In spite of the Prime Minister's visit, and the moon trip, the press paid particular attention to a particular problem in Canada. Everyone admitted there was a problem. The Prime Minister said that he could see the problem. I should like to ask the Prime Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, and the other ministers of the Cabinet, what they consider to be assets of $100,000 in today's economic situation and with today's interest rates.
The present government must accept the responsibility for the high interest rates which now prevail. The Minister of Agriculture is from the same part of the country in which I live and knows full well that interest rates average about 15 per cent, having regard to assets of $100,000. Farmers have to pay anywhere between 8 per cent and 10 per cent on bank loans, and higher rates on borrowings from other sources. Anyone who is operating a wheat ranch, if you would like to call it that, is paying an average of 15 per cent interest on financing.
I pointed out earlier in respect of subsidies that only $29 million of $415 million in Canadian subsidies is being paid to the Canadian wheat grower. This means that over $380 million is being paid in subsidies to people other than wheat growers. Let me bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the Prime Minister are listening to what is being said. It has been suggested that the government does not subsidize people with assets of $100,000 or more, but this government obviously has been subsidizing other industries, including the gold mining industry and the railway companies, to say nothing of the C.B.C. and other Crown corporations. These are virtually monopolies, not prime producers.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is now here and I should like to deal with another subject before I conclude. This minister who has direct responsibility for this subject was recently in Washington. Was the Minister of Agriculture with him at that time?
July 21, 1969
Yes, he was.

Was the Prime Minister with him? The answer is no. I remember an occasion when I spoke in this house when the Prime Minister and the minister responsible for this problem were both in Washington. They conferred with the President of the United States. In the first instance they asked him, "are we friends and allies or are we enemies?" I hope both the ministers realized this. I do not believe that a good purpose can be served at this time by reviewing the international situation and trying to analyze what should be done in those areas where we, as the government of Canada, only have the power to persuade, to discuss, and to try to influence representatives of other governments. I believe that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) adequately covered that in the debate earlier today. However, I believe that an additional explanation should be given of several measures, and of one measure above all others, that this government has taken to alleviate the situation with respect to cash flow through the grain economy in western Canada because of the restricted markets or the contracted markets as compared with a couple of years ago.
It seems to me that the most useful thing that we could do at this stage is. first of all,

I think that all members in this house, even those who come from the grain growing areas in the prairies, will agree that the major problem today is the cash flow in the hands of those people who rely almost exclusively on the sale of wheat and other grains. It is not that they have no product to sell or that their assets have been reduced, bringing them down to the poverty line. The fact of the matter is rather that they have some desperate problems in some cases because the cash flow has been reduced substantially from what it was in 1964, 1965, 1966 and part of 1967. No sooner had we completed the throne speech debate than I drew to the minister's attention serious difficulties in western Canada involving damp grain. Western farmers suffered because their grain was damp. Any grain that had been harvested had not been dried, and any government action had come too late. There was too little of it, and what there was came too late. And what happened, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister went to western Canada and said, "The government can do nothing more." He is lending money, at the expense of the people of Canada, to enable an economy which is sagging badly to continue. There is much that can be done. I would suggest some things if I had time, but I will just make one suggestion now.
More research should be done with regard to the uses of wheat. A day or two ago I heard of some research that had been carried out with regard to the use of fish. The fish are being dessicated, mixed with cereal products and sold or given away under our international give-away program to the hungry people of this world. This product is heavy in protein value. Wheat is the finest protein grain in the world.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
It can be ground up with fish from the maritimes and in that way two problems can be solved. It can be ground and mixed up with codfish and if you do not like codfish,
July 21, 1969

then science can look after that. The taste of the fish can be taken away and it can be made to taste like wheat or pizza or anything you like. There are 40 Ph.D.'s in the Department of Agriculture. What are they doing except emulating the Prime Minister by saying, we cannot do anything about it. Such attitudes do not help one bit in this situation. If there is nothing the government can do about it, then may I say that I, myself, could do a great deal more than the whole tribe over there put together.
Hear, hear.

We do not want a dictatorship in this country, but if we did I would volunteer for the job because I have more brains in my little finger than the people over there have in all their heads put together. I have given them more ideas in the last five minutes than they have had in the last year. I say, give us some reason to believe in you; give us some morale so we can tell our people the Parliament of Canada likes them and wants to do something for them. But let me say that when the government says it cannot do anything, the just society will never be built on that.

Mr. Speaker, it is not often I have the opportunity to agree with the editorial department of the Calgary Herald, but I should like to take my text for this evening from an editorial in that distinguished Conservative newspaper for Saturday, July 19. The editorial entitled "Don't Pretend" reads:
It would be wonderful if oratory could sell Canada's wheat.
Then something worth while might be expected to result from the special debate to be held next week in the House of Commons on the wheat crisis.
But it's no use pretending that rousing words and rolling phrases are going to do the trick. That has been tried countless times before and didn't work. The pages of Hansard that have been filled through the years with words about Western Canada's wheat problems could well command a small fortune as scrap paper.
Unfortunately, the clairvoyance of that newspaper in discerning that a debate would be held here this week was not shared by members of the opposition. Because this party, through its co-operation and concern, permitted the debate to commence early, the opposition speakers were not prepared at all. They simply were not ready and as a result dusted off old speeches and were undeterred by facts relating to what is developing in the world. Furthermore, they have permitted this debate to proceed without the
Wheat Export Prices
hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), St. John the Baptist of the wheat farming people. The hon. member who spoke no less than eight times on the farm credit bill, no less than five times on the farm improvement loans bill, once on the farm machinery syndicates credit bill and four times on the prairie farm advance payments bill, has not been given an opportunity to participate in this debate. I think this is a gross unfairness to him.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) saw nothing wrong with assistance for farmers short of cash, regardless of their substantial assets. Again, if I may, I should like to refer to the editorial in the Calgary Herald, and I agree with it:
It is hard for people to understand why an industry such as wheat farming cannot withstand the economic rigors of one or two bad years like other industries without demanding government hand-outs.
Prime Minister Trudeau said it is hard for a fisherman earning only $2,000 a year to understand why a farmer with land and equipment worth $100,000 should consider himself eligible for government assistance. It is hard to understand because it simply cannot be justified.
The Leader of the Opposition sees nothing wrong with this. I think the perspicacity of the Leader of the Opposition is destined to assure him in his present position at least until he is replaced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) or the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). The Leader of the Opposition does not accept that conditions in the grain industry are the result of international circumstances beyond the control of the Canadian government. With respect I would suggest that the following would summarize the facts of the case.
The last three years have seen excellent harvests throughout the world, mainly as a result of favourable climatic conditions. In each of these three years, world production was higher than in any preceding year in history. Much of this increased production occurred in importing countries whose requirements of wheat were thus increasingly met from domestic supplies. As a result, imports of wheat declined and world trade dropped in the last four years. In 1965-66 world trade totalled 2.3 billion bushels. In the most recent crop year, shipments of wheat were less than 1.7 billion bushels, a reduction of more than 25 per cent.
The drop in world trade in wheat has been matched by an increment in stocks held by the five major exporting countries. On June

July 21, 1969
Wheat Export Prices
30, 1969 these stocks had reached a record level of 2.4 billion bushels. At the conclusion of the Kennedy Round negotiations in the spring of 1967, stocks amounted to only 1.4 billion bushels. In the meantime Canada has maintained its share of the export market at about 20 per cent. Again, gentlemen, I should like to refer to the editorial with which I started:
The best that can be hoped from next week's debate is that it might produce some ideas to assist the government. If so, surely it will be only too glad to accept them.
Unfortunately, the debate may be short on ideas and long on politics.
No amount of talking should be allowed to conceal some important facts. One is that the Canadian government did not create the wheat surplus; it is world-wide. Another is that farmers were warned repeatedly during the bumper-sale years of this decade that they could not depend on Communist countries as steady customers. The big sales to the Soviet Union and China came about because of droughts and wheat-crop failures in those countries. Some of the fat profits from those years should have been used by wheat farmers to branch out into other lines of production.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was caught when the debate was sprung on him a little early. He did not have a single, solitary suggestion. However, this was not so in respect of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). His first suggestion was that we expand the power and authority of the Wheat Board by giving unlimited ability to enter into the price war, with no holds barred. Is that what Canada should do? Are we to take the leadership in this price war? He also wants to reverse the trend to urbanization. He wants to keep the people down on the farm and make sure that the taxpayers of Canada support those who want to stay on the farms. This is really a very progressive move and one, I suggest, we would hardly expect from a member of his party. The third suggestion was that we should accept foreign currency and invest in fertilizer plants. What would these foreign countries which would have these fertilizer plants do with the production they would have? Would they grow grain?
The Leader of the New Democratic party referred to the A.I.D. record and the Leader of the Opposition referred to the acreage payments. I think we might deal with both these at once. I should like to refer to the same O.E.C.D. figures referred to by the leader of the New Democratic party. They indicate that France is first with .95 per cent of IMr. Mahoney.]
its national income devoted to A.I.D., followed by Portugal with .77 per cent and Australia with .74 per cent. One might think it strange to inquire as to how much of France's foreign aid program is devoted to payments of notes due to its colonial empire, how much of that aid goes to north Africa? In the case of Portugal, one might question whether Mozambique or Angola have anything to do with this. In Australia we might think of the Polynesian empire and New Guinea colonies; possibly even the Vietnamese participation.
* (9:10 p.ra.)
The other countries which have any significant amount of foreign aid over that of Canada, are the United Kingdom, Belgium and the Netherlands. This brings us down to 6/100ths of one per cent of the national income over the Canadian contribution. In each case we are dealing with ex-imperial nations, and in each case I suspect strongly that the foreign aid programs are coloured very much by contributions to former colonies.
Le us look specifically at the aid program so far as Canadian grain is concerned. We could increase income by straight payments to farmers or we could increase it by moving wheat through food aid programs or through other subsidies. The opposition continues to refer to the three crop payments of $40 million each it paid to the farmers in 1958, 1960 and 1962, totalling $120 million. In those same years only $66 million worth of grain was moved out in foreign aid. I feel very strongly that farmers would be quite prepared and quite happy, indeed would prefer, to accept a government payment by way of foreign aid than receive subsidies. We also believe in moving wheat and we have done so with our foreign aid program on a scale almost four times as large as that of the previous government.
During the four crop years from 1958-59 through to 1961-62 the foreign aid expenditures in wheat by the Canadian government amounted to something over $66 million. In the most recently completed crop years these have amounted to $240 million, almost four times as much. The total amount of foreign aid, plus crop payment indulged in by the previous government, was about 25 per cent less than the total in foreign aid exports of grain by the present government.
The hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Bigg) in the midst of a diatribe involving the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which quite frankly assumed almost pathological overtones at some points, suggested that the
July 21. 1969

barter system would be a good idea. This is another sort of progressive recommendation from one who avowedly admired the liberalism of Laurier and Gladstone. I am sure that he might have found the conservatism of disraeli and Macdonald somewhat radical even for him.
In any case, the barter system just does not work in respect of commodities as great and as important as wheat to Canada. We cannot possibly get involved in a barter system in respect of our grain or we immediately are going to start facing demands from some of our larger potential customers, and our larger customers in the past including Red China and so on, who are themselves short of cash, who will insist on dealing with us on barter terms when it comes to buying our grain. We must maintain the integrity of our marketing system.
None of this denies the fact that there is a real cash problem which has been well identified by the opposition, for which they are to be congratulated. It would seem from the speeches of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of agriculture (Mr. Olson) that these problems had indeed previously been identified and that many worth while steps had been taken to meet them. However, the cash shortage is there, and certainly some farmers are suffering very seriously.
I do not share the feelings of the Leader of the Opposition that all deserve help regardless of their assets. I do not really believe that we should indulge in this area in another program of universal assistance when we have disavowed such programs for the future in any case. We must provide cash for farmers who find themselves in real need because of the failure of the grain market. We must be selective in this provision and we should, if necessary, resort to a form of means test. I do not think there is much point in trying to solve the cash problem unless we can also try at the same time to solve the market problem.
One thing that the government might consider is the possibility of seeing whether there are not markets for No. 5 or No. 4 grain, which we are not in a position to sell. We could then let our assistance program take the form of paying all or part of the spread between the price we can get for grain of those grades and the value or the price of the actual grades delivered. In this way we might solve both cash and market problems. The types of advances being recommended on acreage payments and so on will leave us
Wheat Export Prices
next spring with the same problem we have today, intensified by whatever surplus we might enjoy from this year's crop, and it looks as though it is going to be a pretty good one.
The two price system has been advocated. Roughly speaking we consume for domestic purposes about 10 per cent of what we have grown in the last few years. The two price system involves fundamentally a tax on the consumer to support the producer in this area. Once this idea is introduced, it will be a simple matter to sit here regularly in this House of Commons listening to the extent of the grain farmers plight and determining just how much the city and town dwellers are going to be taxed by way of extra cost for their bread in order to make up this difference. I think the two price system is a very dangerous thing, and we should avoid it altogether if we can.
Certainly, the long range solution is diversification. This has been recognized by such eminent authorities as Premier Ross Thatcher and the Hon. Alvin Hamilton, a man who is at least regarded in some quarters as being an expert in this area. Certainly, a reduction of wheat acreage is absolutely essential.
I do not see that our economy can possibly support a U.S. type system under which we would be making continuous payments to maintain land out of production. I do not see why we cannot utilize the same sort of programs here that are utilized in the maritimes, and places where industry has fallen into distress, where relocation grants are given to people who are willing to change their vocation. It is questionable indeed that taxpayers should have to pay for something that farmers might well have done for themselves and which, in many cases, progressive farmers have in fact done. These are not miners or people employed in Cape Breton coal mines. These are basically self-employed businessmen, with wide discretion as to how they should handle their affairs. When they find themselves in some trouble we very definitely must give them assistance, but the programs that we advocate in this area must be selective; they ought not be universal.

After listening to that last word of authority on this problem, I am somewhat taken aback. I felt that this was perhaps another Senator in the making. One of the suggestions he made was that there was a need for some sort of assistance to the western economy. Naturally, this would include the province of Alberta. The

hon. member suggested that we should be very selective. Does his reasoning also relate to old age security, which is paid to millionaires? Is that the type of reasoning he has in mind, and does this apply across the board? Is this Liberal policy that is being enunciated, because apparently the member has been selected as one of the spokesmen from the west.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) suggested that only 25 per cent of the loan payments were not made as of the date they were due. If he would look up the previous record, he would find that about a year ago only 6 per cent of the loans had not been repaid. There has been a great increase in unpaid loans. Let me say further that the irresponsible statements have been made to the effect that the former minister of agriculture said "You grow wheat and we will sell it". There could be no more irresponsible statement than the one that came from the lips of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he said, "We intend to sell one billion, three hundred million bushels in three years". Nothing of the sort came about. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) tried to explain to us why this goal could not be achieved now. He said this was a kind of goal, but this is not an election year.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce attempted to chastise the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for having made only one suggestion in his speech, that is for only advocating cash advances for the purpose of injecting money into the western economy in a hurry. Let me say that the only thing with which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) dealt in his speech was cash advances. If anyone can find anything else in his speech, apart from a lot of words, then let him stand up and say so. I think it is somewhat unfair of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to accuse the Leader of the Opposition of having dealt with only one subject in his speech.
Many suggestions were made from this side. I realize that I have only a limited amount of time at my disposal and therefore I should like to organize my comments somewhat. First, I wish to list some of the ways in which the government could inject money into the western economy, money which even the Prime Minister himself admits is needed there. After about three days of indoctrination, and after having seen for himself what

the situation was like, he was ready to admit there was a problem. If the meetings which we had in Saskatchewan with the members of the touring agricultural committee were not sufficient evidence, and if the representations to the government by various farming organizations were not sufficient proof for the Prime Minister, then I don't know what proof he needs. He was going to use the charm he possesses, Trudeaumania-mania it is, but not the type of mania he thought. He believed all he had to say was, "follow". They socked him right there, and he said, "whoa, there" instead of "follow".
The first thing I would suggest, regardless of what anybody else may say here is acreage payments. The Prime Minister asked, "why should we subsidize a rich farmer who possesses $100,000 worth of property?" It is all right provided there is a ceiling, and it is up to the government to select that ceiling. The point is to inject some money into the economy in the west. What the government does not realize is that it is not only the farmers who are broke; it is everybody down the line. The businessmen in the west have gone broke and so have the municipalities which have had to hold back plans for new roadways. The hospitals have had to hold back their projects. The people are sitting and wondering what kind of government we have. I regret to have to say this, Mr. Speaker, but-
Be careful, now.

I am very careful. I say this because I heard it. People are saying that this government turns only one way. They spend $200 million on the city of Hull, and people are asking why the government does not spend $30 million in western Canada. I will make a suggestion as to how this could be done. The International Grains Arrangement price for wheat is $1,951. In recent days this price has gone down by ten cents to $1.85. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce indicated that he sold only 305 million bushels. Is $30 million too much to spend on the three prairie provinces? Is this too much to ask of this government? Do we have to drive a tractor over the Prime Minister before he realizes that assistance is needed? What the government must realize is that these people do not want to act the way they did when the Prime Minister visited them. In the past they have not acted that way because there was no need for it.
I will speak about the Farm Credit Corporation now. In the last four or five years
July 21, 1969

almost $1,100 million has been borrowed from the Farm Credit Corporation. I believe that at present the figure stands at $1,070 million. But the significant fact is that almost one third of that sum has been borrowed in Saskatchewan. The reason is that the people there are more desperate, as is obvious from the statistics. When the people of Saskatchewan did not give the Prime Minister the type of treatment he would have liked to have had, it was not because they are less kind than other Canadians but because they are more desperate. The Minister of Agriculture suggested that cash advances will help them. I say to him, let him come and make a few Liberal speeches in my constituency. I invite him to do so. Let him tell the farmers in my riding, who last year had dry crops and this year had frozen crops, how they can get a cash advance. What is he going to inject there? I know what he is going to inject.
We ask for the adoption of a two price system. It is too much to ask? What is all the talk about guaranteed income? Does it mean something or does it not? Is it or is it not part of the Liberal philosophy? Let the government adopt it if that is what they believe in. Let them go ahead and increase family allowances. It is the families with children that will eat the bread, so let us give them more. But do not deny assistance to those people who have been working hard. I do not think everyone realizes how much work farmers have to do. When you realize that they have borrowed to the hilt and worked their fingers to the bone, there is little enough reward. It was the Conservative government which increases the amount of available loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, but it was the Liberal government that increased the interest on the loans. There lies the difference. At one time the interest rate was 5 per cent. Now, when you go to a bank, you are told "I do not think I will renew your loan because you are a bad risk".
At one time the banker used to say to you, "you are a good risk. Any amount of loan you want is fine". This is not the case now. How can you sell your wheat? The credit is not there any longer. What should the government do? They should make arrangements with these banks, and this can be done, to make loans available at rates lower than they are at present. At one time the interest rate on a loan was 6 per cent, but later it went up to 12 per cent-even 15 per cent as my seat-mate has suggested. That is why there is a shortage of money in the west. No one can tell me that farmers do not need the money,
Wheat Export Prices
but the fact is that the banks have slowed down the granting of credit. These people will not add to the inflation any spiral. They are simply trying to regain credit facilities. They are trying to repay their notes at the bank so they may establish credit with which to carry on. As has been suggested, they will carry on because there is no more enterprising individual than the farmer.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Hear, hear.

The government makes no effort to solve the problem, despite the banks' earnings being at the highest level on record.
I put those figures on record about six months ago and shall not repeat them now because my time is limited. The fact is that the banks have made a great deal of money from the farmer, because he is a continuing borrower. The government must realize that when the farmer goes to the bank, this kind of arrangement is made. What is regional development all about, if it is not to help those areas which are in need? If this is the kind of development we need, the government must institute a program to implement it.
I do not know what I have to do or say to convince the government of the seriousness of the problem. If it is necessary to get down on my hands and knees to do so, I will do it. Does the government realize how many farmers are broke? They are not able to buy groceries. The grocer who allowed them an advance for a month or two is no longer extending this privilege. The situation is extremely serious.
The government says that in three or four months time it will give the farmer a cash advance. I will arrange for the Minister of Agriculture to visit my constituency and explain the government's stand to my people, because an explanation is vitally necessary. I have tried to explain these things to my constituents. I ask the minister to persuade the government to do something to solve this problem and upgrade its image in the west.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) visited my area and knows the type of people I represent. They welcomed him. They spoke kindly of him and to him. Would he please appeal to the Prime Minister, on behalf of these people, to do something to solve the problem? We do not have surpluses. My area developed after the 1930's. There are in Canada depressed areas in provinces other than Quebec. My people cannot

July 21, 1969
Wheat Export Prices
understand assistance being concentrated in one area. It has been said that $125 million was written off in respect of Expo. This was great for Canada, but it did nothing for me or my constituents. It does not enable a family to go to the grocer and obtain a pound of coffee without paying for it. The farmers in my area cannot get their tractors out of the repair shops. Their business suddenly collapses, and some people wonder why. The banker says to him: If you cannot pay up, sell your tractor.
The government has tried to establish economic units. We thought we had economic units. If a farmer is not able to sell his grain, he does not have an economic unit. The Prime Minister has said that if the farmer does not have an economic unit the government will buy his land. Does this offer apply to a man who is unable to sell his grain?
There are on the other side of the house good Liberal backbenchers to whom constituents have opened their books and exposed their income tax returns. This is not an easy thing for people to do because their business .dealings are private, but it has been done. 1 appeal to the government: Let us not be wishy-washy. Let us not be silly about cash advances. There has to be an injection of money into areas of the country which are worse off than others.
I have never opposed anything I believed was good for the country. If a program has been necessary for the maritimes, I have suppported it. Let us not ignore the plight of the western farmer. Let us not delay taking action for political reasons, because later may be too late. If action is not taken now, Canada win lose its best farmers. This is a question of simple mathematics: if you have 1,000 acres under cultivation-this is a much greater acreage than the average farm-and a five-bushel quota, you produce 5,000 bushels, which if sold at $1.70 a bushel amounts to $8,500. One pays about $2 an acre in taxes, and at least $1,000 for fertilizers. The average farmer pays from $1,500 to $2,000 for fuel. If one obtained a loan of $15,000 under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the interest at 5 per cent is $750, which for five years amounts to $3,750.
In addition, a farmer has to pay for repairs to machinery; he has to have enough money on which to live; he has to pay insurance premiums and many other things. The only way one can live on a farm at this time is to send your wife, if she is healthy enough, to work off the farm so she can make some 
money in order that the family may eat. This is the seriousness of the present situation with a five-bushel quota. A $290 million reduction in the final payment last year, compared with that of the previous year, and a reduction of $80 million in sales this year, amounts to $370 million. As I have said, the farmer's costs have increased.
I should now like to deal with the International Grains Arrangement. I believe I understand the situation in this regard. If under this arrangement we have not been able to produce a satisfactory deal for Canadian farmers, we had better scrap it. I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce a question today about the International Grains Arrangement. According to the fine print of that arrangement, members of the European Economic Community are allowed to deduct from the price-

Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for its indulgence. I shall finish my remarks very quickly. France is a member of the International Grains Arrangement. France is our big problem in this regard because she is a large producer and is a supporter of the price level. She has the right to subtract the cost of the freight from the gulf to the port of export and establish her price at that level. Then, France has to add the charge from Marseilles to, say, somewhere in Turkey. This is always lower than the price at the gulf. This is why France is in a preferred position, and her exports are 30 per cent higher this year. But Canada cannot benefit from the same kind of arrangement. I realize that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce does not want to reveal the fine print, but the government had better face up to the fact that Canada has had the wool pulled over its eyes once again. In fact, Australia is now doing what France is doing.

speechtext: We finally have an N.D.P. member in the house.

I hear some comments from across the way, Mr. Speaker, and it is nice to know that government members do have something to say. Except for the tractors that were purring up and down the roads of Saskatchewan last week, the silence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been deafening.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
The Prime Minister was
listening.

Mr. George Bain of the Globe and. Mail said that he had made some remarks about kicking a small boy in his posterior, though I do not know whether that is correct or not.
If hon. members across the way will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some remarks about the grain situation in Saskatchewan and particularly in my constituency. I listened to the bland remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) as he talked of cash advances. Certainly, he must have been in a different part of western Canada from the region I visited last week. Surely, as he watched the television and saw, as I did 7,500 farmers gathering in Regina, another 8,000 or 10,000 gathering in Saskatoon and the thousands of tractors driving up and down the roads, it must have been brought home to him that something was amiss on the prairies.
Today I was informed that the price of wheat has again declined. The members have repeatedly asked over the last several months for a policy statement from the government with regard to meeting the existing situation. Neither the members nor the farmers have received an answer. In view of the situation
in Saskatchewan, I would say that the farmers of that province treated the Prime Minister very well.
I asked the Acting Prime Minister last week whether it was the intention of the Prime Minister of Canada, when he visited Saskatchewan, to meet with the National Farmers Union officials. I was told that no such arrangement had been made. If the farmers union had not put those tractors on the road and made a protest, I submit the Prime Minister would have gone to Saskatchewan, entering on the one side and leaving on the other, without sitting down and talking with the representatives of thousands of farmers in the province.
I like to hear talk of participatory democracy but I am not interested in gobbledy-gook. If the term "participatory democracy" is to be used, let it be used in its real sense. In order to have real participatory democracy the government must be prepared to sit down with the individuals in whom the farmers have confidence, those they have elected to head their organizations, organizations to which the farmers pay a certain amount every year as members.
Eventually the Prime Minister did meet these officials, and we heard talk of farmers with assets of $100,000. This was supposed to be an indication that these farmers were well off, rich. This is the application of the new economics. I did not have the advantage of going to a school of economics to learn about such things, but I have talked to a good many economists and I never thought that one judged a person's income by the amount of capital he was able to invest. But it seems that you do judge the financial position of farmers in Saskatchewan, in Ontario, or for that matter in the maritimes, on the basis of how many tractors they have, the size of the tractors that are standing in the yard, and the acreage that they have.
In all sincerity, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he use a different yardstick, because this one is going to lead him badly astray. The measure of a grain farmer's income is well known. It is measured by how much grain he sells and by the price at which he sells it. The same is true of a livestock farmer. One member on the other side of the house stated that the problem facing the farmers would still exist no matter which government was in power. I do not think the problem would be quite so bad as it is under this government. The difference would be that something would be done to solve the
Wheat Export Prices problem, and this would be quite an important difference.
I should like to tell the government why this is not the first time that the farmers of Saskatchewan and western Canada have found it necessary to demonstrate when a Liberal government was in power. The same thing occurred in 1946. The farmers picketed the grain elevators and dairies in western Canada, and I was one of those who took part. Circumstances at that time had become so intolerable that the farmers just could not make a living. A few years following the action that we took in 1946 the government was bounced out of power, a very prominent minister of the day having tapped a Manitoban on the tummy and told him that he looked very well fed. Perhaps the farmers look well fed, but I am sure the government knows that the credit unions are strapped for resources to make loans in Saskatchewan at this very moment. Surely, the government's sources of information are as good as mine. Surely, the government knows that banks are being selective in granting loans. They must have this information if they are trying to assess what is the present financial situation of the farmers.

I hope the government will take an honest look at the situation and consider just what is at stake at the present time. What is at stake is the economy of the province of Saskatchewan in particular, that province being the main wheat producer, and that of its two sister provinces of Manitoba and Alberta. Some business people have asked prairie provincial governments to clamp a moratorium on interest rates. This is a business economy and when certain people ask for a moratorium to be clamped on interest rates it is time that the powers that be took notice, because something adverse obviously has happened. The government's real failure is in coming to grips with the existing situation. The Prime Minister has told us we must grow less wheat. He could have saved himself the trip to Saskatchewan if that is all he wanted to tell us. The farmers of the country have reduced the acreage of wheat under cultivation from 29 million acres to 24 million acres in one year, which is a pretty hefty reduction. What are they to grow if they do not grow wheat? That question must be answered by the government and farm organizations. Why has the government not consulted with farm organizations and worked out these matters? 

the country are on a four bushel delivered quota right now; others are on three bushels; other areas have delivered five bushels.
